about: The words of the chain great_army_865 (Data/encounters/chain_great_army_865_793.json; Design/content/chains/great_army_865.md): the great heathen army in England, 865 to 880. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', and '...out_<option>_success' and '..._failure' for a chance, named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the news items the cards post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People: the ealdorman Alfred of Surrey and his wife Werburg are historical (the inscription in the Codex Aureus); King Alfred, King Edmund, Guthrum and Bishop Waerferth are spoken of and never met. Toki the weigher, his sister's son Tofi, the boy Wulfric, the priest Hunsige and every unnamed reeve, priest, clerk, dealer and chief are ordinary invented people. Nothing is quoted: the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, the Codex Aureus inscription and the treaty of Alfred and Guthrum are given in our own plain rendering, in the Chronicle's voice where a card states a fact. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: Money for peace
The heathen army sits on Thanet, and the men of Kent have promised it money to stay there. The reeve is collecting. So is a Dane with a pair of scales.
The men of Kent have promised them money for peace. Every hide pays, and every keel that lies here. I did not make the bargain. I only count it.
They say it buys us the winter. I say a wolf does not sell the sheep it means to eat.
Malt, oats, ale, bread. I pay in silver by weight, and I do not care whose face is on it.
Look at the scales if you doubt me. They are honest. It is the only thing in this army that has to be.
Your boat sits low. I can make her sit higher.
Pay twenty pennies into Kent's share

You pay. Within the month the army steals inland by night, under cover of the peace, and harries all the east of Kent. The money was promised and the burning was done anyway. The reeve does not forget who paid while it still looked like sense.
Sell the Dane your ship's own ale and bread at three times their worth
He weighs out cut silver: half an arm-ring and nine pennies of three kings. Your men drink water as far as the next port and say so. The Dane says his name is Toki, and that an army eats every day.
Keep the hatch shut and watch how he weighs

You sell nothing and learn something. He tests each coin with a knife's point and throws back the bad ones without anger. From his talk the army means to winter among the East Angles and wants horses: fodder will be dear there.

Dusk on the Wantsum shore at Sarre in autumn: an English reeve with a tally stick and a sack, and across a trestle from him a broad Dane holding up a small folding balance; far off over the flat island a line of camp fires under a low red sky.
The king's horses
The great army has taken winter quarters among the East Angles. The king has made peace and given them horses. Outside the town the camp trades like a market, with a Dane at the scales.
The king has given them horses so that they will ride away on them. That is the whole plan. I have heard worse ones.
Somebody will ask me how many they are. I have counted three times and had three answers.
The man from Thanet. Sit down. An army remembers who was there early.
A Frisian. Good. Frisians ask the price before they ask whose side I am on.
Iron. Bars and rivets. We have more keels to mend than this shire has smiths, and the smiths have all gone deaf.
These are my weights: lead, with a piece of somebody's book clasp set in the top so I know them for mine. Silver from the east, silver from the Franks. It all weighs the same.
Sit two days at his scales and learn the weights and the words

Two days. You learn the ertog and the ore, how to nick silver, and what a Dane calls a bad coin. You learn that Toki has a sister's son in the fleet and no wish to farm. Your men are bored and say so.
Take his order: six bars of iron, brought here before the army rides
He gives you earnest silver, a cut dirham and some pennies, and scores the order on a stick in marks you cannot read. Six bars before the army rides, at more than half again the price.
Tell the king's man what you saw of them in Kent

You tell him: the peace in Kent, the money promised, the night ride after. He hears you to the end. 'So they take the price and the goods both,' he says. He pays you for the news and looks no happier for having bought it.

A winter camp outside Gipeswic on a grey morning: a ditch and bank, tents of sailcloth, English grooms leading a string of horses in through the gap; in front a Dane seated on a sea chest with a folding balance and a row of small lead weights on a board.
The strand at York
The army holds York. On the strand by the Foss the people taken in the fighting stand roped in a line, and a dealer walks along it naming prices.
All Saints' day. They were at their prayers or at each other's throats, I forget which. Nobody was on the wall.
They had two kings here and were fighting over which. Now they have none, and it is quieter.
A grown man, forty pennies of your money. A woman who weaves, more. I take silver by weight or wine by the cask.
This one reads. A bishop's school, he says. Sixty, because somewhere there is a priest who will pay a hundred.
I can say the psalter as far as the fiftieth psalm, and I write a fair hand. My master is dead in the church porch. Nobody is coming with a hundred.
Buy the boy free and give him a place in the boat
Sixty pennies, weighed. The rope comes off. He says his name is Wulfric. He eats like two men, and by the river mouth he is reading your tally sticks aloud and has found a mistake in them.
Buy four of them for the market over the sea
Four, at thirty each for taking them together. They sit in the hold and do not look back at the town. At Sliesthorp they are worth half as much again, and you will know what you carried.
Buy no one; ask who was taken, and carry the names south
The boy gives you eleven names and whose kin they are. You cannot write them, so he makes you say them back until you have them. Somebody in the south will pay nothing for this and be glad of it.

The muddy strand by the Foss at York under the broken Roman wall, a cold bright noon: a dozen roped people, among them a thin boy of twelve with ink on his fingers; a fur-capped dealer points along the line with a stick; smoke over the town behind.
The king is dead

This winter the army rode back across Mercia and sat down at Thetford. King Edmund fought them, and the Danes had the victory and killed the king. At the landing a priest has a sack he will not put down.
Nine days after Martinmas. They killed him and they hold the land, and there is nobody now to give them horses to go away.
How he died I did not see, and I will not tell it as if I had. In a few years everyone will have seen it.
A chalice, a paten, two book covers. I buried them once. The ground keeps things from Danes and from nobody else.
I buy church silver by weight. What it was for does not weigh anything.
You know my scales. Buy from me and not from the men with the axes. I at least give change.
Take the priest and his sack over to Kent

He comes aboard with the sack between his knees and keeps it there. For Canterbury, he says, where there are still walls and an archbishop behind them. He pays in prayers and promises you both kinds are good.
Buy the camp's church silver by weight

Two pieces, a cup with its foot hacked off and a dish with a lamb on it, for their weight in silver and no more. Whole, in a Frankish bishop's town, they are worth three times that. The priest watches you carry them down to the boat.
Hear it told and carry the news
You hear it three times from three men and it has already begun to grow. What does not change: the king is dead, the army will eat the shire bare this winter, and corn is dear.

A frozen landing on the Orwell at first light: a priest in a patched cloak clutching a heavy sack to his chest; a Dane at a trestle with scales, a hacked silver cup in the pan; on the bank behind, ravens in a leafless tree and smoke rising inland.
The golden book

The army has come from Reading to London for the winter, and the Mercians have made peace with it, which means paid. In the camp by the old walls the Dane with the scales has something wrapped in a cloak.
My bishop has let land at Nuthurst go for twenty mancuses of gold to pay his part. He had it written in the charter why, and in which winter, so that nobody later thinks he was careless.
Every keel on the strand pays toward the town's share. Thirty pennies, and you trade this winter under the army's peace, such as it is.
Gold letters on purple skins, and painted men with wings. Nobody here can read it and every man wants to hold it. That is worth something.
Gold for gold. Not silver: I have silver. Somebody among the Christians wants this back more than I want to keep it. Find him.
I show it to you because you know a true weight. The others would cut it up for the clasps.
They are cutting dies down the street for whoever holds the town. A king's name is the cheapest thing on a coin.
Carry word of the book to Kent
He lets you turn three leaves. Purple and white by turns, and the writing like poured gold. You cannot read it either. At Canterbury there are people who can, and who have gold of their own.
Buy it yourself: four hundred pennies' weight of silver

He wanted gold and takes silver, a great deal of it, because silver in the hand outweighs gold at Canterbury. The book goes aboard wrapped in your spare sail. It is the dearest thing you have ever carried, and nearly the lightest.
Pay thirty pennies to the town's share and trade under the peace
The clerk writes you down. The army will drink the town dry by Candlemas, and anyone with ale to sell does well. The book stays in its cloak. Somebody else may carry word of it, or nobody.

Inside the broken Roman wall of London on a winter afternoon: a Dane on a sea chest opening a cloak to show a great book, its page purple with gold letters catching the light; a tonsured clerk with a wax tablet looks away; tents and tethered horses among fallen masonry.
Pure gold
At Canterbury the ealdorman Alfred and his wife Werburg have heard that the heathen army holds holy books. A priest of Christ Church brings you to them.
You know their camp and the man with the scales. We know only that the books are there, and that they are being handled.
My wife and I will not leave holy books among heathens longer than it takes a boat to fetch them. That is all there is to say about why.
Pure gold, our own, weighed here before the priest. Carry it, bring the book, and he goes with you to see both done.
You have it aboard? Then name your price before I see it. Afterwards I shall not bargain well.
The priest you brought over from the East Angles sits at our table. He has told us what kind of man came for him.
Carry their gold to the camp and bring the book back
Werburg counts the gold out herself, thirty mancuses, into a leather bag that the priest ties to his own belt. His name is Hunsige. He has not been in a boat before and means to pray the whole way.
Sell them the book: six hundred pennies, in gold

Twenty mancuses, weighed. More than you paid, and less than the camp would have had from them. Werburg unwraps the book on the table and nobody speaks for a while. The priest washes his hands before he touches it.
Keep the book for a market over the sea

You say it is not for sale here. The ealdorman says nothing. The priest says a good deal, and it will be said again in every minster from here to York. Somewhere in the north a king who cannot read will pay well for gold letters.
Say it is not your errand
They thank you coldly and send for another shipman. Whether he ever sails you do not hear.

A timber hall at Canterbury by lamplight: a grey ealdorman standing, his wife Werburg seated at the table weighing gold coins in a small balance, a priest holding open a leather bag; the merchant in sea clothes just inside the door.
By weight
In the camp at London the gold is laid on one side of the scales and the book on a chest beside them. The priest stands witness. A chief of the army has come to watch, which was not agreed.
Thirty of their gold pieces was the word, and I keep my word, because next winter I shall want to sell again.
The book is the army's, not the weigher's. A priest has come all this way for it. Then it is worth more than was said.
He will take the thirty if you do not flinch. He only wants to see whether you do.
I am here to see it done, and to say afterwards that it was done honestly. I should be glad to be able to say so.
Weigh out the thirty as agreed and take the book

Thirty mancuses, piece by piece. The chief shrugs and goes to find something else to be owed. The priest carries the book to the boat in both arms like a child, and at Fordwic the ealdorman's man pays your passage without being asked.
Beat the price down and keep what you save
You get it for twenty-five, and the priest watches five gold pieces go into your purse. He says nothing. He will say it at Canterbury.
The chief takes your haggling for an insult to his book. It costs the thirty, and forty pennies of your own to smooth him. The book goes home all the same, and the priest saw you try.
Leave the camp with the gold and without the book

On the river you take the bag and put the priest ashore at the first landing. Thirty mancuses is a year's good trading. The book is cut up for its gold before spring or carried north whole, and your name is read out in chapter at Christ Church, though not for prayers.

The London camp at midday, snow on the ground: a folding balance on a chest with gold coins in one pan, the great book lying closed beside it; a Danish weigher, a tall chief in a wolfskin with his thumbs in his belt, and a small priest gripping a leather bag.
The oath on the ring
The army slipped past the West Saxon host into Wareham. The king made peace with it: hostages given, and oaths sworn on their holy ring. At Hamwic the king's reeve wants a man who knows the camp.
They swore on their holy ring, which they have done for no people before. Then they rode for Exeter by night. I should like to know what the ring thinks of it.
We hold their hostages. I am told each is a great man's son. You have sat in their camp: which of these would be missed, and which are grooms in borrowed cloaks?
Their ships met a storm off Swanage. A hundred and twenty lost, they say. The sea is the only ally the king has not had to pay.
I fell behind on the Exeter road with a lame horse. It is the horse I blame.
I held a broken oar from dusk until morning. If your god sent that wind, he was not aiming at me in particular.
You sat at my mother's brother's scales among the East Angles. He said a Frisian learned the weights in two days and the words in none.
Tell the reeve truly which hostages are men of weight

You walk along the hostages with the reeve and say what you know: this one's father commands ships, that one mucks out. He pays you a hundred pennies from the king's chest and writes down which to guard and which merely to feed.
Buy the young Dane out and set him on the road to his kin

The reeve sells him as he would a salvaged spar. The young man's name is Tofi. He does not thank you at length. He says his mother's brother will hear of it, and that in the army a thing heard is a thing owed.
Sell your cargo and stay out of kings' business
The king's host has been in the field since harvest and must be fed. Corn is dear at Hamwic and will be dearer nearer Exeter. That is all of the war that is your business.

The shore at Hamwic on a windy autumn day: a king's reeve in a good cloak with a wax tablet, a row of Danish hostages sitting under guard on a beached boat's rail, one young man with a blanket round him set apart; grey water and a wreck's ribs beyond.
No ale for Yule
The army has gone into Mercia for the winter and sits at Gloucester. Its buyer is in London with a great deal of silver, buying as no camp buys that means to sit still.
Oats, and more oats. Hard bread. Spare girths. Whatever a horse and a rider need for a week on a frozen road.
Ale? No. Where we are going the ale is already brewed. A king's steward has seen to it.
You have not heard me say that. A man who sits at scales all day talks to keep warm.
Winter at home, Frisian. Do not be in Wessex after the twelfth night. I tell you that for nothing, which you know is not my custom.
You bought me off that beach. So: when the Christians are sleeping off their god's birthday, we ride. Keep your boat out of their rivers.
Carry it to the king's reeve at Hamwic
You load nothing and take the ebb. It is a bad season for the Foreland and a worse one for being believed: all you have is a buyer's shopping and a remark about ale.
Sell him the fodder and ask nothing

Every sack of oats on the strand goes through your hands to his, and you take a tenth for the trouble: a hundred and sixty pennies in cut silver. He does not say where the horses are going. You do not ask.
Not your war: lay the boat up for the winter

You winter where nobody is riding anywhere. After Twelfth Night the army comes down on Chippenham, and the king goes into the marshes with a small band. You hear it at Candlemas, from a man who had it from another.

The Thames strand at London in hard frost, late afternoon: sacks of oats stacked high beside a Dane with scales and an open silver chest; a string of pack horses waiting; no ale cask anywhere; breath smoking in the cold.
Before Twelfth Night
The king's reeve at Hamwic is keeping Christmas. The king keeps his at Chippenham. You have a buyer's shopping, a remark about ale, and as much of the reeve's patience as a tide lasts.
Nobody rides at midwinter. Armies sit by their fires until the grass grows. That is how it has been every year of this.
But you told me true about the hostages when I had no way to check it. Say it again, slowly.
And I do not know you. A Frisian who trades in their camp comes to tell me where they will ride. Why should that not be their errand?
You are too late with it. They came down on Chippenham after Twelfth Night, and the king is in the marshes with a few men. I wish you had rowed harder, or that I had listened sooner to somebody.
Tell it all: he knows what your word is worth

He sends two riders before you have finished your ale, by different roads. When the army comes down on Chippenham after Twelfth Night the king is not at table. He is on the hill behind the town with the men of Wiltshire, and the gates are shut.
Swear to it on his relics

You swear on a saint's finger in a silver box. The reeve watches your hand, not your face, and then calls for a rider. When the army comes to Chippenham the king is not there to be taken, and his men are.

You swear. He thanks you, feeds you, and sends nobody. After Twelfth Night the army takes Chippenham and the king flees to the marshes. When you next meet the reeve he remembers exactly what you said, and on which day.
Say nothing after all; sell and go
You talk of the price of corn. Whatever is going to happen in Wessex happens without you.

A reeve's hall at Hamwic on a midwinter night: a Christmas table half cleared, the reeve leaning forward on his elbows, the merchant standing wet from the sea with his hand on a small silver reliquary; through the open door a groom saddles a horse by torchlight.
The king was not at table
This year, after Twelfth Night, the army stole to Chippenham, and the king was there before them with his host; and at Easter they made peace. The reeve has a chest from the king, and a writing.
The king asked who brought the word. I said a Frisian. He asked whether you could be paid or only thanked. I said you were a Frisian.
They gave hostages and swore again, and this time the king chose the hostages himself, from a list. You will know whose list.
They know somebody talked. They do not know who. I would not sit long at their scales.
Take the king's silver and his protection

Six pounds of pennies and sixty over, in a chest two men carry, and a writing which says that you and your heirs trade toll-free at Hamwic under the king's hand, and that whoever harms you answers to him. You cannot read it. Every reeve in Wessex can.
Ask for land by the water in place of half the silver

Three pounds of pennies and thirty over, the same writing, and a plot above the tide line with the king's stake at each corner. The reeve says a man with a house here will be slower to sell news to the other side. He says it kindly.
Not yet: let it lie with the reeve
The chest goes back under the reeve's bed. He says it will keep, and that kings forget more slowly than merchants think.

The hall at Hamwic on a bright summer morning: an iron-bound chest open and full of pennies on the table, the reeve holding out a sealed strip of parchment, the merchant with his cap in his hand; through the door, ships on the Itchen and a peaceful shore.
Written above and below
At Christ Church the ealdorman Alfred and Werburg give the golden gospels to the community. Their gift is being written into the book itself, above and below the gold letters, in plain English.

It says they bought these books from the heathen army with their own pure gold, for the love of God and their souls' need, and would not leave them in heathen hands. It says nothing of boats. Books never do.
The book does not name you. I do. There is gold set aside, and the community has something to add to it.
I told the chapter how the weighing went. All of it. They have decided to be grateful for the book.
Your Wulfric reads better than half our brothers. That is praise of him and a complaint about us.
Stand witness and take what is offered

Forty mancuses from the ealdorman's own chest. The community writes your name among its friends, to be prayed for by name, and at the ealdorman's word the king's reeve lets your keel lie at Fordwic free of toll for as long as your house sails. The book is laid on the altar. It will be read from every month.
Ask one thing more: that Wulfric be freed at the altar as your foster-son

The archbishop hears who paid sixty pennies for a schoolboy on the strand at York and asked nothing for it since. The community doubles the ealdorman's gold: eighty mancuses. Wulfric is freed at the altar with the gospels open, and it is written in the book's margin that he is free and of your house. He reads the line out to you twice.
Not yet: you have a tide to catch
The priest says the gold will keep and the prayers have already started, whether you stay for them or not.

Christ Church at Canterbury, morning light through a narrow window: the great book open on the altar at a purple page of gold letters, a scribe bent over it writing small dark words in the upper margin; the ealdorman and Werburg standing with their young daughter, the merchant a little apart.
Hostages at the Lea

King Alfred and King Guthrum have a peace, and a border up the Thames and up the Lea. No man, free or slave, may go over to the other army without leave. But if they must trade, in cattle and in goods, it is allowed when hostages are given.

Englishmen I cannot send: half would not come back, and the other half would come back with wives. Danes I will not let in. A Frisian is nobody's man. It is the first time I have heard that said as praise.
Leave a pledge with me, so that both sides know you go with a clean back. You have it again when you come over the water with what you said you would bring.
The Frisian. Good. I have land now, and a wife who says it wants ploughing. I would rather buy and sell. Bring cloth. I have horses, and more silver than sense.
On the other bank they still ask who talked before Chippenham. Nobody here knows. Keep it so.
Leave sixty pennies as your pledge and take the leave to cross

A season of crossings: English cloth and wine one way; horses, hides and weighed silver the other; and few others allowed to carry them. Seven hundred pennies clear when the pledge comes back. The reeve gives you a tally cut with the king's mark. It is the whole of the law, and it fits in a purse.
Stand surety for other Frisian keels too, with Toki to answer on the far bank

Your pledge covers four keels, and each pays you for the cover. Toki keeps your goods on the Danish side under his own roof and answers for them with his land. A thousand pennies clear by the year's end. On both banks they begin to say 'ask the Frisian', which is a title of a kind.
Not yet: let others try the crossing first
The reeve shrugs. The river will still be a border next year, he says, and the year after.

The mouth of the Lea where it meets the Thames, a still grey morning: an English reeve at a post on the near bank holding a notched tally, the merchant's boat loaded with bolts of cloth, and on the far bank a Dane with horses on a rope, raising one hand.
The land shared out
This year the army went from Cirencester into East Anglia, and settled the land and shared it out. Toki, who never wished to farm, has a share by the river and no use for it.
They have given me land for fifteen winters at the scales. I asked for silver. They said the land is the silver now.
Our king has been under the water and come up with an English name. He strikes pennies with it. I weigh them like any others.
You sold to us when nobody knew how it would end. There is a plot by the landing with my mark on the post. Put a house on it and we are fellows: your keel, my scales.
The gold book went north with a man bound for Sliesthorp. I hear a king there shows it to his guests and holds it the wrong way up.
Tofi has the next share to mine. He says you are owed a horse. He has no horse. He will.
Take the plot and Toki's fellowship

You strike hands on it before witnesses, in the Danish fashion. The plot is forty feet of river bank with a post on it. Toki weighs out your part of fifteen winters' dealing, nine hundred pennies of cut silver, and loads a second boat that sails when yours does. The English priests of the shire know whose fellow you are.
Take your part in silver, and no land among them

He is not offended. He weighs out fourteen hundred pennies, some of it still shaped like altar furniture, and takes you before the king who was Guthrum, who gives you guest-right in his land: a seat, a hearing, and nobody's hand against your keel. The English priests of the shire know where your silver came from.
Not yet: see first whether their peace holds
Toki says the post will stand. He has put it in deeper than he puts most things.

The river bank at Gipeswic on a spring evening: a new post with a mark cut in it on a strip of bare ground, a Dane grown grey shaking hands with the merchant over it, a plough leaning unused against a new timber house, two boats drawn up side by side.
This year the heathen army sat on Thanet, and the men of Kent promised it money for peace; and under cover of the peace the army stole away by night and harried all the east of Kent.
A great heathen army has taken winter quarters among the East Angles. The king there has made peace and given them horses.
The army holds York. Both kings of the Northumbrians are dead inside the walls, and those taken are sold on the strand by the Foss. A Frisian carries the names of some.
This winter King Edmund of the East Angles fought the army, and the Danes had the victory and killed the king, nine days after Martinmas.
The army swore peace to King Alfred at Wareham on its holy ring, gave hostages, and rode for Exeter by night all the same.
After Twelfth Night the army rode on Chippenham and found the king's host waiting and the gates shut. They say a shipman brought the word.
